ddx.step1_summary:
- Patient: 26-year-old female (Itha)
- Chief complaint: New dry, itchy, red skin on arms and hands
- Onset/duration: Began a few days ago; noticed after a swimming session
- Course/severity: Persistent itch; coconut butter not helping; no mention of cracked skin; no spots
- Associated symptoms: No fever, no sweating, no vomiting, normal appetite, normal bowel and urinary function; feels tired/run-down; otherwise well
- Distribution: Mainly hands and arms; not on chest, legs, or face
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: Temporal association with swimming; work stress increased recently; emollient (coconut butter) ineffective
- Past medical history: No prior eczema or dermatitis reported; possible lactose intolerance
- Medications/allergies: Taking Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive); no other meds; no drug allergies stated
- Family history: Father with asthma; mother with hayfever; no known family skin diseases
- Social history: Primary school teacher; long working hours; high stress; lives alone; non-smoker; no alcohol or recreational drugs
- Vitals/exam: No vitals documented; no physical exam performed in transcript
- Labs/imaging: None

I: Tinea corporis/manuum: Communal exposure (swimming pool) could transmit dermatophytes; itchy, red rash possible though distribution and rapid onset are less typical.
Scabies: Intense pruritus and hand involvement are possible, but lack of nocturnal itch, burrows, or contacts makes it less likely.
D: Xerosis cutis (dry skin) due to weather/low humidity: Patient suspects weather; dry, itchy skin on exposed areas is consistent.
Nutritional deficiency (e.g., essential fatty acid deficiency): Can cause dry, scaly skin, but acute onset over days and otherwise good health argue against it.
I2: Irritant contact dermatitis from chlorine/pool chemicals or frequent handwashing/soaps: Onset after swimming; hands/arms distribution; dry, red, itchy skin; emollient not yet effective.
A: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to pool disinfectants, fragrances in soaps/shower gels, detergents): Pruritic erythematous dermatitis after exposure; hands/arms commonly affected.
Atopic dermatitis (adult-onset): Family atopy (asthma, hayfever) and stress as triggers; pruritic, eczematous changes on hands/arms.
E: Hypothyroidism: Can cause generalized dry skin and fatigue, but acute localized onset after swimming and lack of other hypothyroid features make it unlikely.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Irritant contact dermatitis (chlorine/pool chemicals or frequent handwashing/soaps)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic temporal relationship to swimming with localized pruritic erythema and dryness of hands/arms; no systemic symptoms; common presentation of irritant dermatitis.
supporting_evidence: Onset a few days ago after swimming
Distribution on hands and arms (areas exposed to water/chemicals)
Dry, itchy, red skin; no fever or systemic signs
Occupational hand-washing as a teacher could contribute
opposing_evidence: She has swum before without issues (suggests not a new exposure, though concentration/skin barrier changes can alter response)
Coconut butter emollient not helping yet

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to pool disinfectants, soaps, detergents, fragrances)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Pruritic eczematous rash after exposure; hands/arms are common sites; could be to pool chemicals or personal care products used around the time of swimming.
supporting_evidence: Itchy, erythematous dermatitis limited to exposed areas
Family history of atopy may predispose to contact sensitivity
opposing_evidence: No vesicles or well-demarcated borders reported

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Pruritic eczematous dermatitis with family atopy and recent stress; hands commonly involved in adults.
supporting_evidence: Family history: father with asthma, mother with hayfever
High stress, which can precipitate flares
opposing_evidence: No personal history of eczema; first episode at age 26
Acute onset after a specific exposure (swimming) suggests contact dermatitis
Not classically flexural and limited to hands/arms

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Xerosis cutis due to weather/low humidity
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry, itchy skin on exposed limbs can be from environmental dryness; patient suspects weather.
supporting_evidence: Patient reports belief it may be weather-related
opposing_evidence: Erythema suggests dermatitis rather than simple xerosis
Short time course of only a few days

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dermatophyte infection can be acquired from communal facilities and causes itchy, red, scaly lesions.
opposing_evidence: Diffuse involvement of both arms and hands rather than annular plaques or unilateral hand involvement
Patient reports no 'spots' and no classic ring-like lesions
